newsitem.title: PERU: Chronology of Peruvian hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Peruvian hostage crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stunned the world on Dec. 17 when they stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and took about 500 hostages.
Here is a chronology of the main events so far in the crisis, which entered its 12th day on Sunday.

TUESDAY, Dec 17 - About 20 heavily armed guerrillas blow a hole in the wall at Japanese ambassador's Morihisa Aoki's home at 8 p.m. EST (0100 GMT) and swarm in to capture around 500 people, including government officials and foreign diplomats, attending a cocktail party. The rebels release about 80 women and elderly people in the hours soon after the attack.

WEDNESDAY, Dec 18 - MRTA guerrillas inside the residence threaten to kill their hostages unless the government frees up to 500 jailed comrades. But they let pass an ultimatum to kill Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela unless Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori personally talks with them.

THURSDAY, Dec 19 - Four ambassadors are released to set up a "communications channel" between the rebels and the government, but their role is quickly sidelined. Fujimori assures U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of the hostages is his first priority.
FRIDAY, Dec 20 - The rebels release 38 hostages and promise to free another "significant" number. In a statement, they repeat their demand for MRTA prisoners to be released.

SATURDAY, Dec 21 - In conversations from within the residence, captives Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela and Japanese Ambassador Morihisha Aoki say the hostages are being treated well and urge the government to open a dialogue with the rebels. Fujimori, in his first public words since the crisis began, says he will not use force and will study a non-violent "way out" if the guerrillas lay down arms and free all hostages.

SUNDAY, Dec 22 - The guerrillas release 225 hostages not linked to the government as a "Christmas gesture" but vow to keep the remaining 106 as bargaining chips to pressure for the release of MRTA members in jail. Remaining hostages include President Alberto Fujimori's brother, top government officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen, and a handful of Asian and Latin American ambassadors.

MONDAY, Dec 23 - Released hostages tell of overcrowded, unhygienic conditions inside building, but also of gentlemanly, disciplined rebels who debate politics and economics wearing explosives on their backs. An international MRTA spokesman in Germany says the rebels will never surrender, while police fear another clandestine MRTA cell might be waiting in Lima for retaliatory attacks in case the government storms the residence.
TUESDAY, Dec 24 - Red Cross officials deliver Christmas cake, and a Jesuit priest held hostage conducts a Mass. The rebels release Uruguay's ambassador after his country frees two MRTA prisoners.
WEDNESDAY, Dec 25 - The remaining 105 hostages suffer a grim Christmas Day, but Japanese diplomat Kenji Hirata is released in a wheelchair due to his delicate condition.

THURSDAY, Dec 26 - An explosion at the residence in the early hours shatters the Christmas lull, but Red Cross officials later report there are no injuries. The explosion is eventually attributed to an animal stepping on a rebel-placed mine. Guatemalan ambassador Jose Maria Argueta is freed as an "acknowledgement of the peace process" in his country.

FRIDAY, Dec 27 - Fujimori extends state-of-emergency rule to cover the whole of Lima as a consequence of the crisis. The Group of Seven (G-7) industrialised nations condemn the rebels as "terrorists" and pledge to help Peru by all "appropriate" means.

SATURDAY, Dec 28 - Government negotiator Domingo Palermo enters the residence for the first face-to-face negotiations with the MRTA. The meeting is followed by the release of 20 hostages and a conciliatory rebel statement expressing willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."

SUNDAY, Dec 29 - Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto welcomes signs that a peaceful solution might be possible, but warns against over-optimism and says the remaining 83 hostages are still enduring a "tough situation."
